Despondent

/dih-SPON-dent/ — stress on the middle syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Despondent describes someone who feels deeply discouraged and has lost hope, often after a disappointment.

After failing his driving test for the third time, Marcus grew despondent and stopped practicing.

Worked Example

After being rejected from her top five colleges, a senior stopped checking her email, withdrew from her friend group, and told her parents that college didn't matter anymore. She had become despondent.

Being 'sad' or even 'disappointed' doesn't capture what happened here. Despondent is more precise because it means she didn't just feel bad—she lost hope altogether and gave up trying. The disappointment crushed her spirit, and that total loss of hope is exactly what despondent means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dejected: Dejected means sad and sunk low in spirits after a letdown — slumped shoulders, a heavy quiet. It describes the mood of a bad day or week. Despondent goes further: the person has not only sunk low but lost hope and stopped trying. Dejected is how you feel; despondent adds the giving up.

demoralized: Demoralized means drained of confidence and fighting spirit, the way a team feels after losing badly — the will to keep pushing has leaked away. Despondent is more personal and darker: hope itself is gone, not just morale. A demoralized player doubts the next game; a despondent one no longer sees a reason to play.

forlorn: Forlorn means sad in a lonely, abandoned way — a forlorn figure waiting alone on an empty platform. The word leans on isolation and desolation. Despondent centers on crushed hope after a disappointment: a despondent person can be surrounded by supportive friends and still be unable to believe anything will get better.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

optimistic: expecting things to turn out well

buoyant: cheerfully upbeat and hard to discourage

Where it sits · how completely someone has given up — disappointed → discouraged → despondent → hopeless

disappointed vs. despondent: Disappointed is far weaker than despondent — disappointment is the sting of one letdown, while a despondent person has lost heart about the whole road ahead.

discouraged vs. despondent: Discouraged is weaker than despondent; a discouraged person doubts whether the next try is worth it, while a despondent person has stopped trying altogether.

hopeless vs. despondent: Hopeless is even stronger than despondent — the despondent person has lost heart and given up for now, while the hopeless person believes no improvement is possible at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: away, down (Latin)

Root — spond

Root — spond: to promise, to pledge (from spondere) (Latin)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: in a state or condition of (adjective-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin despondere joins de- ('away') with spondere ('to promise') — literally to promise something away, to give it up. A despondent person has signed away their hope and lost heart.

Use the root in a new word: sponsor

Use the root in a new word: sponsor: A sponsor is someone who promises to support a team or event — the same root spondere, 'to promise,' hiding inside despondent, where hope has been promised away.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Despondent is the deep discouragement of a broken spirit. Reach for it when someone has lost hope, not just faced a setback. For everyday disappointment or low motivation, 'discouraged' or 'disappointed' is simpler.
